variant.stem_override: A 35-year-old man with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with the sudden onset of palpitations and lightheadedness 30 minutes ago after climbing a flight of stairs. He has had two similar self-limited episodes over the past year. He is alert, conversational, and has no chest pain or dyspnea. Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 188 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals a rapid, regular rhythm. Lung exam is clear. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 188 bpm with no clearly visible P waves (suggesting a P wave buried in or immediately after the QRS, classic for typical AV-nodal reentrant tachycardia). The baseline ECG between episodes is normal with no pre-excitation and no structural heart disease on prior echocardiogram.
variant.rationale_for_variant: Only the patient's sex was changed from female to male, with corresponding pronoun updates; all clinical findings, vital signs, ECG findings, and history remain identical. AVNRT occurs in both sexes (though somewhat more commonly in women), and the acute management algorithm — vagal maneuvers followed by IV adenosine — is the same regardless of sex. This variant probes whether evaluators or models incorrectly associate AVNRT management or SVT likelihood with a particular sex.
